title: The Strong City Falls and the Poor Give Thanks
english: … of others, that Satan has been called a city, and a strong one at that. For it is the custom of the God-inspired Scripture at times to liken the very mightiest to towers and walls, or even to cities. So, as we said earlier, even the blessed prophet Jeremiah was set by God as a fortified city and as a strong bronze wall (Jeremiah 1:18). But when Emmanuel was revealed and shone upon the world, the unholy throng of the opposing powers was destroyed, and Satan was shaken from his very foundations. He has fallen so as to sink into endless weakness, and he has no hope of ever rising again or lifting up his head.

“Therefore the poor people will bless you, and cities of men who are wronged will bless you. For you have become a helper to every lowly city, and a shelter to those who lost heart through want; you will rescue them from wicked men. A shelter for the thirsty, and the breath of men who are wronged. They will bless you as faint-hearted men who thirst in Zion, from ungodly men to whom you handed us over” (Isaiah 25:3–5).

Israel was called to the knowledge of God through the tutoring of the Law, and was made rich in the things that come from God; for it was saved, and inherited the land of the promise. But the countless multitude of the other nations, I mean those throughout the whole earth under heaven, had been utter strangers to the spiritual goods from above. They had no taste of the gifts that come from God. They were, in a way, naked and unclothed, having neither the divine shelter nor the covering from on high, neither the wealth of mind that comes from virtue nor anything else of all that is full of praise and counted worthy of every wonder. But when Christ himself appeared, he took them out of the devil’s grasping and brought them to God the Father. They have been made rich with the light of the truth, with a share in the glory that comes from him, and with the greatness of the gospel way of life; and for these things they send up songs of thanksgiving to God the Father.

So then, he says, O Master, since you have carried out an ancient and true counsel (Isaiah 25:1), summing up all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10), enlightening those in darkness and casting down the world-rulers of this age (Ephesians 6:12), strong as cities though they were, the poor people will bless you, and whole cities will glorify you. For you have become a helper to every one of them, and a shelter to those unbearably grieved by their poverty in the goods of their fathers; and you rescued them from wicked men. For in Zion too there were some who had lost heart in this way, just like men who are thirsty. And perhaps by these words the prophet shows us this: there were, yes, there were in Israel too those who thirsted for the Savior’s coming, and the Savior of all …

translator_notes: The section opens mid-sentence (ἄλλων, 'of others') and ends mid-word (κα…); both breaks are marked with ellipses and nothing is supplied.

Jeremiah: τέθειται … ὡς πόλις ὀχυρὰ καὶ ὡς τεῖχος χαλκοῦν ὀχυρόν matches LXX Jeremiah 1:18 (τέθεικά σε … ὡς πόλιν ὀχυρὰν … καὶ ὡς τεῖχος χαλκοῦν ὀχυρόν). It is Jeremiah whom God sets as the fortified city.
ἐξ αὐτῶν … βαράθρων [al. βάθρων]: the edition's alternative βάθρων ('from his very foundations', i.e. utterly) is followed; the printed βαράθρων would give 'from the very pits'.
Isaiah 25:3–5 is quoted in its LXX form; πνεῦμα ἀνθρώπων ἀδικουμένων is 'the breath of men who are wronged' (passive participle).
καίτοι καθάπερ τινὰς πόλεις οὕτως ἰσχυράς is read as a concessive phrase on τοὺς κοσμοκράτορας ('strong as cities though they were'), which picks up the opening image of Satan as a strong city.

title: Prayer for Peace with God
english: It is the custom of the holy prophets to make supplications on behalf of Israel. For they were lovers of God and richly crowned with the glories of piety. And since they had sprung from the root of Abraham and from the blood of the holy fathers, they are of necessity downcast when they see those of Israel, as their own kin, perishing because of their impiety toward Christ. For this reason the blessed prophet Isaiah now comes forward and says: “Lord our God, give us peace; for you have rendered all things to us” (Isaiah 26:12). For if you grant us peace, he says, we shall be full of every good thing, and we shall have received in full the most perfect share in your gifts.

We must consider what kind of peace they ask for. Either they ask for Christ himself, for he is our peace, according to the Scriptures (Ephesians 2:14), and through him we have been joined to the Father, by kinship, that is, spiritual kinship. Or at least they mean this: those who have not yet believed, and whose stain of sin has not been cast off, stand apart from God and are rightly reckoned in the rank of enemies; they hold their necks high and fight against the laws of the Master. But those who are obedient and easily led, and ready for anything at all that those laws approve, are very dear to him and have peace with him. Yet this thing is truly given by God and comes through the generosity from above. Grant us, then, O Master, to be at peace with you, and, once profane and loathsome sin has been taken out of the way, to be united to you spiritually through Christ the Mediator.

Such is the word rightly spoken through the voice of Paul: “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). When this has come about, we shall be God’s possession and his inheritance. That is why it is wisely added: “Lord, take possession of us; apart from you we know no other; we name your name” (Isaiah 26:13). For those who are at peace with him must be single-minded and yoked to God alone, so as to know him only and not even to carry on their tongue the name of any other, falsely named god at all. For we must name him alone, because he alone is God over us by nature and in truth. The law of the all-wise Moses proclaimed something of this kind to us: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve, and by his name” (Deuteronomy 6:13; compare Matthew 4:10). Amen.

“But the dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up. Therefore you brought it upon them and destroyed them, and took away every male of theirs. Add evils to them, Lord; add evils to all the glorious of the earth” (Isaiah 26:14–15).
Those who know only him who is God by nature and in truth, and who name his name, and reckon to him …
translator_notes: The section opens on the broken end of Isaiah 26:13 (…αμεν, the end of οἴδαμεν); only the intact clause 'we name your name' is translated. The section ends mid-sentence after ἐπαριθμοῦντες αὐτῷ; nothing is supplied.
πεφήνασιν ἐκ ῥίζης Ἀβραάμ has the prophets as subject: they themselves are of Abraham's root and blood, and so grieve for their kin.
τῶν αὐτοῖς ἀρεσκόντων: the plural αὐτοῖς is taken to refer to the nearest plural, the Master's laws ('whatever those laws approve').
φιλοτιμία here is God's generosity, not 'ambition'.

Deuteronomy 6:13 is quoted in the form Matthew 4:10 gives (προσκυνήσεις … μόνῳ); 'and by his name' keeps Cyril's shortened end of the verse. Ἀμήν stands inside the edition's quotation marks but is not part of the verse; it is kept after the citation.
Isaiah 26:14–15 is quoted in its LXX form (ἰατροί, 'physicians'; ἐνδόξοις, 'the glorious').

title: The Lawlessness of Jacob Taken Away
english: “… stones of the altars broken to pieces like fine dust; and their trees will not remain, and their idols cut down like a forest far off” (Isaiah 27:9).

Having set in between his reproof of those who had acted impiously toward the holy prophets, the blessed prophet again holds to the sequence of his thoughts, and says, as from the person of God: “Therefore the lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away” (Isaiah 27:9). “Therefore”: for what reason? Because he will not be slain as he himself slew, nor struck as he himself struck (Isaiah 27:7). For the gentleness that is in God always overcomes human pettiness; he does not in every way and in every case bring penalties equal to the offenses committed on earth, but rather tempers his wrath with mildness.

This is why he says: “The lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away”; that is, he will receive loving-kindness, and God will in due time remit his charges and free him even from the accusations themselves. “And this is his blessing.” For God promised Abraham, saying: “Surely I will bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed” (Genesis 22:17). But the godlike Abraham would not truly have been blessed, nor would his seed have been multiplied, if those of his blood had been required to pay penalties in proportion to their sins. But since they too, though they had done nothing good, and had rather been carried down into the utmost impiety, were enriched with forgiveness, the ground of the blessing has been kept and has passed on to them. “When, therefore, I take away his sin,” he says, “this will be the manner of his blessing.”

He also makes plain the time at which Jacob too will be free of his offenses. For when, he says, those called through faith to the knowledge of him who is truly God take the field against the ancient error; when altars and sacred precincts and the swarm of idols are taken out of the way; when they consume with fire the temples built with toil for lifeless idols; when they cut down their trees, and besides these the things made with hands, like a forest: then, then indeed God will remit their stumblings to those of Israel as well. And this, I think, is what the godlike Paul declared: “But when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26).

For to burn the temples down completely, to shear off the groves planted beside them, and to add as well the overthrow of the statues themselves, would signify nothing else, surely, than this: that those who long wandered in error and worshipped the works of their own hands will be changed and come to the knowledge of the truth, and will reach such love of God as even to lay hands on the things they once worshipped, and those of …
translator_notes: The section opens mid-word (…ίθους, i.e. λίθους, 'stones') inside the Isaiah 27:9 lemma and ends mid-word (τοὺς ἐκ ξ…, probably 'those of wood'); the breaks are marked with ellipses and nothing is supplied.
Isaiah 27:7 (μὴ ὡς αὐτὸς ἐπάταξε … καὶ ὡς αὐτὸς ἀνεῖλεν, οὕτως ἀναιρεθήσεται) is the verse Cyril answers in 'he will not be slain as he himself slew'.
ἀνήσει (from ἀνίημι) means 'remit, let go' (of charges and stumblings), not 'raise up'.
Genesis 22:17 is quoted in Cyril's shortened form (Ἢ μὴν εὐλογήσω σε).
ἔφησε φῶς ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος: φῶς appears to be a printing slip and is not translated. The Pauline quotation spans Romans 11:25–26 (πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέλθῃ … πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ σωθήσεται).
